title: Chariot Racing
objective: After this level you can describe chariot racing, the Circus Maximus and the racing factions.
summary: The Circus Maximus held about 150,000 fans. Four color factions raced four-horse chariots seven laps, and rivalries could turn into riots.

cards.headline: Rome’s biggest crowds didn’t watch gladiators. They watched chariots.
cards.body: Rome had a venue that made the Colosseum look small. And its fans turned out to be more than spectators.

cards.headline: The Circus Maximus
cards.body: The Circus Maximus, Rome’s great racetrack, could hold about 150,000 spectators, about three times the Colosseum’s 50,000. A standard race was seven laps around the central barrier, the spina. The most prestigious races used quadrigae: chariots pulled by four horses. Seven laps, four horses, and a crowd the size of a city.

cards.headline: Reds, Whites, Blues and Greens
cards.body: Charioteers raced for four factions, the Reds, Whites, Blues and Greens, and each faction had passionate fans. Sound familiar? It’s the ancient version of wearing your team’s colors. A charioteer who won often enough could become rich and famous. The first sports celebrities drove at a gallop.

cards.fact: Racing fans nearly toppled an emperor.
cards.context: In 532 CE, fans of two factions, the Blues and the Greens, rioted together in Constantinople. The Nika revolt nearly toppled the emperor Justinian. When sports fans can shake a throne, they’re a political force. Not bad for a day at the races.

questions.explanation: There were four factions: the Reds, Whites, Blues and Greens.

questions.prompt: Match each name from chariot racing with what it was.
questions.explanation: The spina was the central barrier of the track, quadrigae were chariots pulled by four horses, and the Nika revolt of racing fans nearly toppled the emperor Justinian.

questions.prompt: From Level 56: the Colosseum held about 50,000. How many times more could the Circus Maximus hold?
questions.explanation: About 150,000 spectators is roughly three times the Colosseum’s 50,000.
